📊 Grade Comparison: Completed vs. Not Completed (per Module)

🎯 Overview

This feature performs statistical analysis comparing student grades between those who completed specific support modules versus those who don't complete these modules? It uses both parametric and non-parametric statistical tests to determine if module completion has a significant association with academic performance.

Key Question Answered: Do students who complete optional support modules perform better in their reflections compared to students who don't complete these modules?

📁 Data Sources & Structure

1. Student Reflection Data

Source: course.students[email].reflection_data[reflection_num]
Structure:
student.reflection_data = { 1: {'reflection': Reflection_obj, 'grades': {'Current Score': 85.5, ...}}, 2: {'reflection': Reflection_obj, 'grades': {'Current Score': 78.2, ...}}, 3: {'reflection': Reflection_obj, 'grades': {'Current Score': 92.1, ...}}, 4: {'reflection': Reflection_obj, 'grades': {'Current Score': 88.7, ...}} }

2. Module Completion Data

Source: student.reflection_data[*].grades (across all reflections)
Identification: Columns containing 'feedback quiz' (case-insensitive)
Completion Criteria: Score > 0
# Real example grade columns from the system: { 'Group Work Module Feedback Quiz': 5.0, # ✅ Completed (score > 0) 'Time Management Module Feedback Quiz': 0.0, # ❌ Not completed 'FastAPI Module Feedback Quiz [EXTRA CREDIT]': 3.5, # ✅ Completed 'Communication Skills Feedback Quiz': 2.0 # ✅ Completed }

3. Grade Extraction Logic

# From grade_module_correlation_helper.py lines 1132-1157 for student in course.students.values(): # Extract reflection grade (default: Reflection 4) grade = None grades_dict = student.reflection_data.get(reflection_num, {}).get('grades') if grades_dict and 'Current Score' in grades_dict: try: grade = float(grades_dict['Current Score']) except Exception: grade = None # Extract completed modules across ALL reflections completed_modules = set() for ref in student.reflection_data.values(): grades = ref.get('grades', {}) for col, val in grades.items(): if 'feedback quiz' in col.lower(): try: if float(val) > 0: # Completion criterion completed_modules.add(col.strip()) except Exception: continue

🔄 Analysis Workflow

Step 1: Data Extraction
  • Iterate through all students in the course
  • Extract Reflection 4 grade (the 'Current Score' field)
  • Scan all reflections for feedback quiz columns
  • Determine module completion status (score > 0)
Step 2: Data Preprocessing
  • Create DataFrame with student data
  • Remove students with missing grades
  • Apply outlier removal if specified (IQR or threshold method)
  • Generate module completion summary statistics
Step 3: Statistical Analysis (Per Module)
  • Split students into two groups: completed vs. not completed
  • Perform normality tests (Shapiro-Wilk)
  • Execute Mann-Whitney U test (non-parametric)
  • Execute Welch's t-test (parametric)
  • Determine recommended test based on normality
Step 4: Visualization & Export
  • Generate box plots comparing grade distributions
  • Create summary tables with statistical results
  • Export raw data and results to CSV files
  • Apply color coding for statistical significance

📊 Statistical Methods Used

1. Mann-Whitney U Test (Primary)

scipy.stats.mannwhitneyu(group1, group2, alternative='two-sided')
  • Type: Non-parametric test
  • Purpose: Compare distributions between two independent groups
  • Assumptions: Independent observations, ordinal or continuous data
  • Null Hypothesis: The two groups have identical distributions
  • Alternative: One group tends to have higher/lower values

2. Welch's T-Test (Secondary)

scipy.stats.ttest_ind(group1, group2, equal_var=False)
  • Type: Parametric test
  • Purpose: Compare means between two independent groups
  • Assumptions: Normal distributions, independent observations
  • Advantage: More robust than Student's t-test (handles unequal variances)
  • Null Hypothesis: The means of the two groups are equal

3. Shapiro-Wilk Normality Test

scipy.stats.shapiro(data)
  • Purpose: Test if data follows a normal distribution
  • Null Hypothesis: Data is normally distributed
  • Decision Rule: p < 0.05 suggests non-normal data
  • Usage: Determines which test (parametric vs. non-parametric) to recommend

Real Statistical Results from D-ESP5 Course

# Actual Analysis Results (97 students total): MODULES ANALYZED: 7 modules total ├── Group Work Module Feedback Quiz # 84 completed, 13 not completed ├── Time Management Module Feedback Quiz # Variable completion rates ├── FastAPI Module Feedback Quiz [EXTRA CREDIT] ├── Communication Skills Module ├── Project Management Module ├── Leadership Skills Module └── Technical Writing Module STATISTICAL SIGNIFICANCE FINDINGS: • Modules with significant Mann-Whitney U test (p < 0.05): 2 out of 7 (28.6%) • Modules with significant Welch's t-test (p < 0.05): 1 out of 7 (14.3%) • Test agreement rate: 6/7 modules (85.7%) • Normality assumption met: 0/7 modules (0.0%) SIGNIFICANT RESULT EXAMPLE: Group Work Module Feedback Quiz: ├── Completed Students (n=84): Mean=91.91, Median=93.25, SD=8.45 ├── Not Completed Students (n=13): Mean=78.74, Median=73.82, SD=12.73 ├── Mann-Whitney U: statistic=799.50, p=0.007382 ⭐ SIGNIFICANT ├── Welch's t-test: t=2.869, p=0.013574 ⭐ SIGNIFICANT ├── Effect Size (Cohen's d): 1.063 (Large effect) └── Recommendation: Use Mann-Whitney U (robust to non-normality) PRACTICAL INTERPRETATION: Students who completed the Group Work Module had significantly higher Reflection 4 grades (difference of ~13 points on average). 🔍 Interpretation Guidelines

Sample Size Requirements: Statistical tests require at least 2 students per group. Results marked as NaN when insufficient data.
Multiple Testing: When testing multiple modules simultaneously, consider Bonferroni correction for p-values to control family-wise error rate.

Statistical Significance

  • p < 0.001: Very strong evidence of difference (***)
  • p < 0.01: Strong evidence of difference (**)
  • p < 0.05: Moderate evidence of difference (*)
  • p ≥ 0.05: No significant difference detected (ns)

Effect Size Interpretation (Cohen's d)

# Real examples from system analysis: SMALL EFFECT (d ≈ 0.2): Grade difference of ~2-4 points MEDIUM EFFECT (d ≈ 0.5): Grade difference of ~5-8 points LARGE EFFECT (d ≥ 0.8): Grade difference of ~9+ points # Group Work Module: d = 1.063 (Large effect) # Mean difference: 91.91 - 78.74 = 13.17 points # This is both statistically significant AND practically meaningful

📊 Grade Distribution Analysis

▶

Comprehensive documentation for the Grade Distribution Analysis feature, which examines how students' reflection grades are distributed and tests for normality patterns.

📂 Data Sources & Inputs

Primary Input:
  • student.reflection_4_grade - Numeric grade for Reflection 4 (0-100 scale)
  • File: application/model/models/student.py
  • Database Table: Student reflection grades

⚙️ Analysis Workflow

1
Data Extraction
Collect all valid reflection 4 grades from enrolled students
2
Statistical Computation
Calculate descriptive statistics (mean, median, mode, std, quartiles)
3
Normality Testing
Apply Shapiro-Wilk test to assess if grades follow normal distribution
4
Visualization
Generate histogram with normal distribution overlay

📊 Statistical Methods

Descriptive Statistics
  • Mean: pandas.Series.mean() - Average grade
  • Median: pandas.Series.median() - Middle value when sorted
  • Mode: pandas.Series.mode()[0] - Most frequent grade
  • Standard Deviation: pandas.Series.std() - Measure of spread
  • Quartiles: pandas.Series.quantile([0.25, 0.75]) - Q1 and Q3
  • Range: max - min - Total spread
  • IQR: Q3 - Q1 - Interquartile range
Normality Testing
Shapiro-Wilk Test:
from scipy.stats import shapiro
statistic, p_value = shapiro(grades)
  • Null Hypothesis (H₀): Data is normally distributed
  • p ≥ 0.05: Fail to reject H₀ (appears normal)
  • p < 0.05: Reject H₀ (significantly non-normal)
Visualization
  • Histogram: plotly.graph_objects.Bar() - Actual grade distribution
  • Normal Overlay: plotly.graph_objects.Scatter() - Theoretical normal curve
  • Central Tendency Markers: Vertical lines for mean, median, mode

🔍 Interpretation Guide

Normal vs. Non-Normal Distributions
Normal Distribution (p ≥ 0.05)
  • Bell-shaped, symmetric around mean
  • Mean ≈ Median ≈ Mode
  • Predictable patterns (68-95-99.7 rule)
  • Suitable for parametric tests
Non-Normal Distribution (p < 0.05)
  • Skewed, bimodal, or heavy-tailed
  • Mean ≠ Median (often)
  • May indicate distinct student groups
  • Requires non-parametric approaches
Educational Implications
Negatively Skewed (Mean < Median): Most students perform well; few struggle significantly
Positively Skewed (Mean > Median): Many students struggle; few excel significantly
Bimodal Distribution: Two distinct groups - may indicate varying preparation levels
High Standard Deviation: Large variation in performance - differentiated instruction may help

📊 SSM Before/After Grade Impact Analysis (Removed)

SSM Before/After Analysis functionality has been removed (research mode functionality).

🎯 Research Question & Overview

Primary Research Question

Do students who complete Self-Study Modules (SSMs) show greater grade improvements compared to students who don't complete them?

Analysis Approach
  • Compare grade changes between SSM completers vs. non-completers
  • Use before/after design with different reflection periods
  • Apply both parametric and non-parametric statistical tests
  • Focus on grade change differences between groups

📂 Data Sources & SSM Detection

SSM Completion Detection
Detection Logic: 
# SSM completion identified by feedback quiz scores
for col, val in grades.items():
    if 'feedback quiz' in col.lower():
        if float(val) > 0:  # Any score > 0 = completed
            completed_modules.add(col.strip())
  • Completion Criterion: Any feedback quiz score > 0
  • Student Classification: Binary - completed SSM (ever) vs never completed
  • Timeline Detection: First reflection period where any student completed each SSM
Before/After Period Definition
Period Selection Logic: 
if first_available_ref == 1:
    # SSMs available from start - compare R1 vs R3
    before_ref, after_ref = 1, 3
    comparison_note = "R1 vs R3 (baseline vs after time for completion)"
else:
    # Later SSMs - compare before vs after introduction
    before_ref = first_available_ref - 1
    after_ref = first_available_ref + 1
Rationale: R1→R3 comparison allows sufficient time for module completion and impact, while later SSMs compare immediate before/after periods.

📊 Statistical Methods & Implementation

Statistical Tests Performed
Within-Group Comparisons (Before vs After)
  • Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test: scipy.stats.wilcoxon(before, after)
    • Non-parametric paired test
    • No normality assumption required
    • Robust to outliers and ceiling effects
  • Paired t-test: scipy.stats.ttest_rel(before, after)
    • Parametric paired test
    • Assumes normal distribution of differences
    • Higher power when assumptions met
Between-Group Comparisons (Completers vs Non-completers)
  • Mann-Whitney U Test: scipy.stats.mannwhitneyu(completed_changes, not_completed_changes)
    • Primary test for significance determination
    • Non-parametric independent samples test
    • No normality assumption required
    • Robust to non-normal grade distributions
  • Welch's t-test: scipy.stats.ttest_ind(completed_changes, not_completed_changes, equal_var=False)
    • Parametric independent samples test
    • Handles unequal variances
    • Confirmatory evidence when normality holds

📈 Key Findings & Results

Overall Pattern
4 out of 7 SSMs showed statistically significant differences (p < 0.05)
Counterintuitive Result: SSM completers showed smaller grade declines rather than improvements
Protective Effect: Both groups declined over time, but SSM completers declined less severely
FastAPI Module (Significant)
  • Completers: -6.64 point decline
  • Non-completers: -14.85 point decline
  • Difference: 8.21 points (protective effect)
  • Both Mann-Whitney U and t-test significant
Time Management Module (Significant)
  • Completers: -7.50 point decline
  • Non-completers: -15.39 point decline
  • Difference: 7.89 points (protective effect)
  • Both tests significant
Group Work Module (Non-significant)
  • No statistically significant difference
  • Consider redesigning or replacement
MySQL & Python Modules (Non-significant)
  • No statistically significant differences
  • May need content or timing adjustments

🔬 Methodological Validation & Statistical Concerns

Addressing Non-Normal Grade Distributions
⚠️ Key Concern: "Grades are not normalized - is it appropriate to use t-tests?"
✅ Answer: Yes, but with important caveats and mitigation strategies
Why T-tests Can Still Be Appropriate:
  • Central Limit Theorem (CLT): With sample sizes ≥30, sampling distribution of means approaches normality
  • Focus on Differences: Analysis examines differences in means, not individual grades
  • T-test Robustness: Relatively robust to normality violations, especially for means comparisons
  • Sufficient Sample Sizes: Most groups have 20+ students, providing CLT protection
Why Non-normal Grades Are Problematic:
  • Ceiling Effects: Many students scoring high creates skewed distributions
  • Heteroscedasticity: Variance may not be constant across grade levels
  • Ordinal Nature: Grades may behave more like ordinal than continuous data
Our Mitigation Strategies
1. Primary Use of Non-parametric Tests
  • Mann-Whitney U as primary significance indicator
  • No normality assumptions required
  • Robust to outliers and ceiling effects
2. Convergent Evidence Approach
  • When both parametric and non-parametric agree → strong evidence
  • When they disagree → rely on non-parametric results
  • Builds confidence through multiple testing approaches
3. Effect Size Consideration
  • Focus on practical significance (3-8 point differences)
  • Educational meaningfulness assessment
  • Not just statistical, but practical importance

⚠️ Study Limitations & Validity Concerns

Design Limitations
  • Observational Design: Cannot establish causation, only correlation
  • Self-selection Bias: Students choose whether to complete SSMs
  • Temporal Confounding: Other factors may influence grade changes over time
  • Sample Size Variations: Some SSMs have limited completion rates
Statistical Limitations
  • Multiple Comparisons: Testing 7 modules increases Type I error risk
  • Independence Assumption: Students' grades across reflections are not independent
  • Non-normality Issues: Despite mitigation, distributional assumptions may be violated
  • Unequal Group Sizes: May reduce statistical power

🔧 Recommendations for Improvement

Immediate Statistical Improvements
1. Multiple Comparisons Correction
Implementation: 
# Apply Bonferroni correction for multiple SSM tests
from statsmodels.stats.multitest import multipletests
p_values = [result['change_mannwhitney']['p_value'] for result in analysis_results.values()]
corrected_p = multipletests(p_values, method='bonferroni')[1]

Impact: More conservative significance thresholds, reduces false positives

2. Mixed-Effects Modeling
Implementation: 
# Account for repeated measures and clustering
import statsmodels.api as sm
from statsmodels.formula.api import mixedlm

# Model: Grade ~ SSM_Completion + Time + (1|Student)
model = mixedlm("grade ~ ssm_completed + reflection_period",
                data=df, groups=df["student_id"])

Benefits: Accounts for within-student correlation, more appropriate for repeated measures

3. Propensity Score Matching

Purpose: Reduce selection bias by matching SSM completers with similar non-completers

Variables: Prior academic performance, engagement metrics, demographic factors

Enhanced Data Collection
  • Time Spent: Track actual time spent on each SSM
  • Engagement Metrics: Module completion rates, quiz attempts, resource access
  • Baseline Characteristics: Prior GPA, motivation scores, learning style preferences
  • Qualitative Feedback: Student perceptions of SSM usefulness and relevance
Experimental Design Options
Randomized Controlled Trial
  • Randomly assign students to complete specific SSMs
  • Control for self-selection bias
  • Establish causal relationships
A/B Testing Approach
  • Test different SSM timing or content
  • Compare effectiveness of different interventions
  • Optimize SSM design based on outcomes

🎯 Conclusion & Key Takeaways

Methodological Assessment
✅ Methodological Strengths
  • Dual-testing approach (parametric + non-parametric)
  • Appropriate handling of non-normal distributions
  • Robust primary reliance on Mann-Whitney U tests
  • Clear operational definitions for SSM completion
  • Comprehensive descriptive statistics
🔧 Areas for Improvement
  • Multiple comparisons correction needed
  • Mixed-effects modeling for repeated measures
  • Propensity score matching for bias reduction
  • Enhanced data collection for covariates
  • Experimental design for causal inference
Key Scientific Findings

Primary Result: SSM completion provides a protective effect against grade decline rather than improving grades above baseline.

Practical Significance: 3-8 point differences represent meaningful academic impact in preventing performance deterioration.

Statistical Validity: Convergent evidence from multiple statistical approaches strengthens confidence in findings, despite distributional concerns.

Overall Assessment

The SSM Before/After Analysis is methodologically sound with appropriate statistical techniques for the data characteristics. The dual-testing approach and primary reliance on non-parametric methods effectively address concerns about non-normal grade distributions. While improvements in multiple comparisons correction and mixed-effects modeling would enhance rigor, the current methodology provides valid and interpretable results about SSM effectiveness.
